Evidence and further reading

Why business discovery comes before AI.

There is no universal AI-project failure rate. These sources use different definitions, samples, and methods. Together, they support disciplined discovery, planning, testing, and human oversight—not a guarantee of success.

Recurring AI implementation barriers

RAND: define the right business problem

RAND interviewed 65 experienced data scientists and engineers. Its industry participants most often identified leadership misunderstanding or miscommunicating the problem, inadequate data, technology-first projects, insufficient infrastructure, and technical limitations.

Read the RAND report

BCG: capabilities separate pilots from value

BCG's 2024 research involving more than 1,000 companies found that 26% had moved beyond proofs of concept and begun generating tangible value; 74% had not. The leaders focused on fewer high-priority opportunities, core business processes, people, and operating capabilities.

Read BCG's report

McKinsey: workflow redesign and operating rigor matter

McKinsey's 2026 survey found that 37% of respondents attributed a positive enterprise-level EBIT contribution to AI, while about 6% qualified as high performers. Those high performers were distinguished by workflow redesign, leadership commitment, and operational rigor.

Read McKinsey's 2026 survey

Planning evidence

Formal planning and venture viability

A peer-reviewed study of 1,088 prospective founders used propensity-score matching and found a 16.1-percentage-point difference in venture viability between comparable formal planners and nonplanners. It concerns new ventures rather than AI and should be interpreted as evidence for disciplined preparation—not a universal success rate.

Read the study by Greene and Hopp

Responsible AI guidance

NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework asks organizations to establish the intended purpose, business value, context, goals, risk tolerance, requirements, limitations, and human oversight for AI systems.

Explore the NIST AI RMF

News examples

  • McDonald's ended an automated ordering trial after real-world errors, illustrating the value of bounded pilots, human correction, and a willingness to redesign.
  • Air Canada was held responsible for incorrect chatbot information, illustrating that accountability does not disappear when automation produces the statement.
  • A Reuters report examined companies struggling to demonstrate returns, reinforcing the need to define outcomes and measurement before scaling.

Claims this project avoids

  • “80% of all AI projects fail.” RAND cited an external estimate but did not independently establish a universal rate.
  • “95% of AI pilots fail.” This viral phrasing often conflates pilots, organizations, production deployment, and financial impact.
  • “A business plan makes any company 16% more likely to succeed.” The academic finding was a matched-sample difference in a specific population and outcome.
  • “Completing this framework guarantees AI success.” Preparation reduces avoidable uncertainty; it cannot eliminate every business or technology risk.
